The breeze of fall intensifies To raw and brisk now, matching our communal moods, And tears at banners left in protests Of a nation keen divided When the thousands marched for social justice While recalling Mr. Floyd. The willows are emitting sighs of deep despair. A sharp-edged crescent moon with sickle points Admonishes: The easy days are past, Stand ready for the rising tides. Is it Lincoln’s statue showing furrowed brow in sudden consternation When confronted by a virus most notorious Locking up our nation’s prized museums And shutting down too many schools As tokens of this viral hour of infamy? Citizens afar are face to face with Frequent fearsome cyclone storms That, one behind the other, rage, While twisters inland Heedlessly devour homes and hospitals. California’s gobbled up by wildfires Leaving ashen villages and vineyards Never burned before, then stuffing in the wake A suffocating smoke to choke the innocent and elderly. The world has stopped abruptly in its tracks. The jovial corner druggist, broke, Closed up his shop for good. Our spunky third-grade teacher with her babe in arms Stood hours long in unemployment lines. We need a spark of newfound courage now emerging From survivors of this snake-bit era, Intently sweeping out the trash of past complacency, Intent to win this battle with Corona. These times will test our fortitude Till peaceful armies of our solons Sound a conch horn to inaugurate a budding era And unleash our nation’s wonders in totality again For all of us to see, assimilate and feel. Posterity awaits to weigh our strength Confronted by tsunamis of adversity. Paul Hertelendy is a classical music and dance reviewer, a published poet, and a Piedmont resident. articles.text: Editor: In 15 years what is the probability that the State will mandate that all non-essential facilities be disconnected from the electrical grid and the natural gas distribution network and either be operated off-grid using energy generated and stored on site or be closed? Will a public aquatic facility be considered essential? What is your level of faith in the unpleasant predictions currently made by the climate models? We should scale down the 2016 vision for our new aquatic facility in order to minimize its energy use. The first question should be, what is our energy budget (measured in MWh not $)? Within that budget which of the many community needs can be met? What can be built and operated now and be made to evolve smoothly in the future, given foreseeable technology improvements? The current on-going process is backward. It was appropriate when resources were infinite and there was no need to choose between powering schools or pools. The one outlined above will ensure that the City can afford the operating costs in the short term and keep the pool open in the long term. Frugality is a forgotten, ancient virtue whose value will become more and more apparent with time. –Bernard Pech For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has experienced a slight increase in crime in July, August, and September compared with the same period in 2020. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers detailed crime data at a city council meeting on November 15. There were 253 reported offenses in the third quarter of 2020, as compared to 267 reportable offenses in 2021, showing a slight increase. Violent crime numbers have remained flat, but the city has seen a substantial increase in larceny theft. In July, August, and September, there were a total of 59 thefts reported to the department. What continues to drive the increase in larceny is the phenomenon of catalytic converter thefts, Chief Bowers explained. The catalytic converter houses precious metals that are harvested once they are stolen. “We caught several people in the process of stealing them, or caught [them] on our license plate readers. It’s something many regional communities are experiencing, and it’s very frustrating. It was not surprising to us to find that there is organization to [the crime].” “We find them, take them to custody, but shortly thereafter [the suspects] will be released,” Bowers said. “If they don’t have a criminal history, they could be released fairly quickly. [Crime] organizations are bailing them out in these catalytic converter thefts.” According to the department’s Uniform Crime Report third quarter comparison, there were more crimes overall in 2020 and 2021 as compared to 2019. There were 86 and 85 reportable offenses in 2021 and 2020, respectively, and 69 in 2019. “To deal with these [issues], the department continues to leverage an awareness that we need to be out-and-about, present, and driving around,” Chief Bowers said. Bowers also credited the departments use of technology, including the Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) program. The department made 24 arrests through the third quarter of 2021, an increase from 14 arrests made during the same period last year. “The APLRs help prevent crime,” Bowers said, a program the city has maintained since 2013. Mayor Teddy Gray King asked Bowers to provide details on the program’s impact, given that safety camera programs can be a divisive issue in some communities. “It’s a tool that is great for law enforcement, but a tool that many people have questions about, and rightfully so,” Bowers said. “We have the absolute privilege to use this [APLR] technology… we have to continue to be as transparent as possible in how we’re using this. That was the thought behind the transparency portal.” The department has maintained a transparency portal for over a year that can be found by visiting https://piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/police/ transparency_portal. The public is invited to provide feedback, comments, and concerns about the ALPR program, in partnership with Flock Safety. The department is currently in the process of implementing a public safety camera program, approved by City Council earlier this year. The current phase of the implementation consists of working with the data fiber provider and utility company to bring the necessary infrastructure to camera locations; Bowers noted the department’s appreciation for the assistance of the city Public Works Department and Director Daniel Gonzales in the process. Juvenile officer Officer Nicole Casalnuovo has rotated out of the Juvenile Officer position which has been filled by Officer Hugo Diaz. Chief Bowers added that school district administrative staff were included on the interview panels and “provided important input in the evaluation” process. “[Diaz] has a substantial background of working with youth, has volunteered with at-risk youth programs in Oakland, and he’s very adept at working with teenagers,” Chief Bowers said. “No surprise, he did exceptionally well in the interviews. The overarching focus and goal is to guide [youth]. Hugo has been great, and his communication with the [PUSD] Wellness Center and school staff has been focused on team-building, to help young people in crises.” The department uses funding from the Department of Justice Tobacco Grant to re-stablish the Juvenile Officer position in 2017. The department reapplied for the grant in 2021 but did not receive funding. Bowers explained that he has maintained communications with the grant administration and intends to reapply during the next filing period.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the Measure UU Bond Oversight Committee. The deadline to apply is Wednesday, December 8, at 5 p.m. The committee will consist of five residents who will focus on review and reporting on the expenditure of the proceeds of the bonds. The bonds for the project will be sold on November 18, and interest on the bonds is tax exempt with maturities ranging from 2023 through 2051. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and activities for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spent in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020. The committee will meet two times per year throughout the project until the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete, which is anticipated to be a 24 to 36-month process. Interested residents may download the Application for Appointive Vacancy and/or apply online on the City’s web site at https://piedmont.ca.gov. Interviews with the City Council for these positions will be scheduled for the evening of Monday, December 13, 2021. No appointments will be made without a Council interview. Residents with questions may contact the City Clerk’s office at 510-420-3040. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: On November 10 the Piedmont School Board approved a universal set of “Single Plans for Student Achievement” goals for all three Piedmont elementary schools. Beach School Principal Michael Corritone presented a report developed by administrators and faculty. Corritone began by reviewing the goals from the last school year, 2020-2021. At that time, the elementary schools’ first goal of Single Plans for Student Achievement focused on continuity of instruction despite online-only distance learning. The second goal was to plan to safely and efficiently switch to hybrid learning. Literacy and mathematics, were the main targets at elementary school last year and were measured by meeting “Essential Learning Outcomes.” “Of course things were unbelievably challenging for everybody,” Corritone stated. “In the end, we were really pleased 85% of students reached those [goals] in mathematics. Those that didn’t meet all those targets were referred to summer school.” The new goals presented showed a marked change from the pandemic-based goals of the previous year. Goal One: “All students and staff will feel physically safe and emotionally supported as part of a caring and inclusive community.” Efforts towards this goal, include the quarterly administration of the Social Emotional Health Screeners. Family Identity Surveys with a diversity, equity and inclusion focus were also sent out at the start of the year. A total of 29% of all elementary school families responded to the Identity Survey which had 12 multiple choice or open-ended questions. On a question regarding a “sense of connection with the community” 30-39% percent responded with either “kind of”, “not very much at all”, or “not at all.” Havens Principal Anne Dolid aims for 50% participation in the next iteration of the survey and less that 10% of families describing their community connection as “kind of”, “not very much at all”, or “not at all.” Goal Two: “All students will engage in relevant learning experiences that foster life-long curiosity, creativity, collaboration, critical thinking, communications and responsible citizenship.” Corritone explained efforts toward this goal included the implementation of a new science curriculum adopted from Carolina Smithsonian. Elementary students have three new units of study: Physical, Earth and Life Sciences. Engineering will be added next year. Goal Three: “Teachers and staff, with district partners will ensure an outstanding educational experience for every student through collaboration, innovation, and professional growth.” These “Single Plans” were primarily developed on Wednesday afternoons when elementary students get out early for staff development.

articles.text: A laser cutter was delivered to the new engineering lab at Piedmont High School’s engineering lab in the STEAM building on November 17. It was in use by students for the past year by Piedmont students in the garage of John Lambert and his wife Helen Potter, key organizers of the Makers group in town. “It was pretty tough to move. It weighs 700 pounds. When we installed it into position in our garage it had 3/4” inch bolts that go down onto the floor, so we had to crank those feet back up onto the casters, prior to moving it,” Lambert explained. With the help of four school district staff members, Lambert and Potter loaded the laser cutter onto a truck for the four-block ride to the high school campus. The machine is a Nova 35, CO2 laser produced by Thunder Laser, capable of cutting anything non-metallic. The laser requires only a regular 120 volt circuit and pulls 100 watts. It cuts by burning through materials at the thickness of a human hair. A separate unit called a chiller cools the CO2 glass tube down so it doesn’t break. An air compressor pumps air through the laser head to keep smoke out of the mirror and a large exhaust fan removes the smoke produced by the burning of the laser. Lambert has been indispensable in the setup process. The laser cutter needed to be perfectly level prior to operation. Since it is now at the school, the power switch needed to need to be replaced for safety with a keyed switch. Lambert ordered the specific part and installed the keyed switch himself. “It took me about an hour to take it apart and replace it, but the school district was extremely happy,” he said. The Makers have mainly been cutting parts for prototyping with the laser cutter out of cardboard, plywood, and acrylic. The actual mechanisms used on Makers robots are easier to produce out of metal or other materials once the prototypes are in hand. The funds for the laser cutter were raised through donations to Piedmont Makers, about $10,000. “This one (cutter) can’t do metal. We are actually looking for one that can, a fiber laser, which is probably our next purchase, but they are more expensive, in the range of $50,000-$60,000,” Lambert said with a smile. Currently, Physics teacher Marna Chamberlain has a guitar-making class that will use the laser cutter. Her class has curriculum relating audio to physics by building speakers. Their class will eventually design and build their own guitars, with the help of the laser cutter. There are many more application for the laser cutter the school can utilize. “We sent the school some examples of a biology teacher who was cutting the shapes of human organs out of felt, and using those to build the intestinal system or circulatory system in biology,” explained Potter. Piedmont Makers has seen exponential growth in participants, and is now has 50 teams and 340 students participating. The addition of the new laser cutter will help answer the swelling demand for more engineering resources in Piedmont. John Lambert (front) and PUSD facility staff carefully position the 700-pound laser cutter onto a lift gate for transport to PHS.

articles.text: Possibility of more than 2,000 runners this year Thousands of people from Piedmont and beyond will converge near Piedmont Park tomorrow, November 25, for the 20th annual Turkey Trot. The 5-kilometer race will begin at 8:30 a.m., and all signs are that it could draw more than 2,000 runners. The popular Thanksgiving morning event took a hiatus last year due to COVID-19 and gathering restrictions. This year, it returns with all the same traditions. Runners will meet before the race begins in front of the Exedra at the corner of Highland and Magnolia Avenues. Coffee and hot chocolate will be served at Corcoran Group, formerly Highland Partners, at the beginning and the end of the race. There will also be plenty of refreshments afterwards. The 5-kilometer race will begin along Highland Avenue and continue onto Wildwood Avenue and La Salle Avenue, before looping back along Sea View and Mountain Avenues. The route is considered a good workout for serious runners and a benchmark for hundreds of others looking to improve their time. For many others, it’s simply a lively social event before the Thanksgiving festivities begin at home. Although anyone can join the race, those who have registered are in the running to win some sweet prizes. (For registration, jersey and bib pickup information, see separate article on page 1.) Winners will be announced at an awards ceremony after the last runner crosses the finish line. Prizes are awarded to the top three runners in each age category, from youth to seniors over 80. All winners will receive a racing cap, a fresh bouquet of flowers from J. Miller Flowers, and a pumpkin pie from Piedmont Grocery. The overall male and female winners will receive a turkey from Village Market, and running shoes from Transports. Proceeds from the Turkey Trot support Piedmont High School cross country and track-and-field teams. The bulk of proceeds are given to the City of Piedmont to fund sports facilities maintenance.

A normal visit to the 2,520- foot summit, such as our visit in March 2020, would be difficult to keep a 6-foot distance for those who are COVID-19 conscious. This time, however, it wasn’t difficult to keep ample space from fellow patrons on the wide gravel trail despite passing 170 hikers on the way up. Instead of the usual mass gathering at the Summit Pole, there were never more than 10 people, giving us a surprising opportunity to snap a few shots. A dozen night-owl hikers were still trekking up to the summit on our way back down. Senior hikers or beginners can find several places to stop on the way up the 3.25-mile trail on the way to Mission Peak, elevation 2,500 feet. With a flashlight in hand, there was never a point when we would get too far ahead or too far behind other hikers, providing a feeling of safety under the night sky. Be sure to pack plenty of water to stay hydrated, add some granola or source of energy, and a charged battery for videos of an unforgettable sunset. articles.text: Stein leads with 2nd place finish; Black, Oesterer qualify as individuals Piedmont’s cross-country teams returned to Hayward High to toe the line for the Division 4 North Coast Section Championship on Saturday, November 20. The boys’ team placed 3rd out of 19 schools and earned a trip to the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park in Fresno this Saturday, November 27. It will be the first appearance at the State Meet for the boys’ team since 2017. The girls’ team narrowly missed going to State, placing 4th among 13 schools. However, its lead runners, Ellie Black and Josie Oesterer, both qualified as individuals. It is the first time in 10 years the PHS girls’ team has not qualified for the State championship. Jack Stein and Ellie Black led the way for their teams, notching personal records in the process. Stein continued a highly successful season by placing 2nd overall in a field of 144 runners with a time of 15:29.4. He improved his personal record time by six seconds, eclipsing Reece Proctor’s time in 2016 by three seconds for the current course record at Hayward High since its reconstruction in 2016. “My goal coming in was to qualify for state with a top-three finish, and I also wanted to beat Reece Proctor’s course record. I was two seconds away in the WACC Championship and I really wanted to get his time. It feels awesome,” said Stein. “Reece’s team was one we all looked up to. He was a star and we heard his name all the time,” added Stein. Crosby Freeman set the PHS record at the North Coast Section meet in 2001 with a time of 15:15. Behind Freeman is Mark Ceraldi in 2005 with a time of 15:24. Stein now ranks in at No. 3 and Proctor No. 4 All-Time at the NCS meet on the course at Hayward, but Stein is now the record holder on the revised course. Ellie Black places 4th at NCS Black was 4th overall among 105 runners, finishing with a time of 18:10.7. Oesterer earned the final qualification spot for Fresno by finishing 12th in 19:07.6. “I definitely looked up the other girls in the race and what their best times were this season, so I kind of knew what to expect,” Black said. “My plan for the first mile was to make sure I didn’t go out too fast and die out in the race. I tried to get up the hills as fast as I could,” she said describing her strategy mile by mile. She missed the early portion of the season rehabbing from an injury, but retuned when she was 100 percent. articles.text: Former Piedmont tennis player Mackie McDonald is currently ranked No. 55 on the ATP World Tour, one ranking below his career high. Without any remaining ATP Tournaments for 2021, the 26-year old pro will return in January 2022 and will undoubtedly appear in the Australian Open on January 17-30. ATP 250 events like the Antalya Open from Jan. 4-11, or the Murray River Open are typical preparatory trials ahead of the Grand Slam in Australia. Since his appearance in the U.S. Open in September, he defeated No. 49 James Duckworth of Australia in the Round of 128 on October 7 at Indian Wells’ BNP Paribas Open. He matched up against No. 2 Daniil Medvedev in the second round on October 9, ultimately losing in straight sets, 6-4, 2-6. At the VTB Kremlin Cup in Moscow, McDonald defeated No. 80 Yoshihito Nishioka on October 20 in straight sets, 6-3, 6-4 in the Round of 32. However, No. 124 Frenchman Gilles Simon upset McDonald in the Round of 16 on October 21. McDonald’s last win came on October 26 in the St. Petersburg Open Round of 32 against No. 113 Egor Gerasimov of Belarus in straight sets, 7-5, 6-4. He lost to Spain’s No. 19 Roberto Bautista Agut in the Round of 16 by scores of 6-3, 6-2 on October 28. McDonald appeared earlier this month at the ATP 250 Stockholm Open in Sweden on November 9, but lost in three sets, 2-6, 6-3, 5-7, to No. 50 Davidovich Fokina in the Round of 32. articles.text: Sophia Zalewski, Piedmont High School’s Valedictorian in 2020 and its record-setting distance runner, throughout high school, was part of the team from Carnegie Mellon that placed third at the Div. 3 Mid-Atlantic Region Cross-Country Championship on Saturday, November 13 at Big Spring High School in Newville, Pennsylvania. She placed 22nd in a field of 216 runners with a time of 24:23.7. Her team qualified for the Division 3 NCAA Cross Country Championship one week later. Her team placed 18th of 32 schools on a 6,000 meter course at Tom Sawyer Park in Louisville, Kentucky. Zalewski finished 187th among 292 runners with a time of 23:01. She is competing as a freshman after the fall 2020 season was wiped out due to the global pandemic. “It felt really great getting to run at nationals and be part of such a strong team. Our woman’s team this year is the best it’s been in a long time, and it’s really encouraging to know I am contributing to that and getting to race with a great group of girls,” she said. Zalewski’s emergence on the program wasn’t without adversity. She required seven months to heal from a stress fracture, and rehabbing during a global pandemic thousands of miles from home added to the frustration. Zalewski returned to running in the middle of the season and competed in just a couple of events prior to the Mid-Atlantic Championship meet. “It felt great to race again for the first time since before COVID Sophia Zalewski ran with Carnegie Mellon at the Div.3 Cross Country NCAA Championship in Louisville, Kentucky on Saturday, November 20. and be part of the team environment that I love so much. Making the nationals team was very motivating. It was so much fun to run with a team again and get back in the competitive mindset,” she added. During her high school career in Piedmont, Zalewski typically competed in 5,000-meter events. She is the school’s all-time record holder on nearly every course, including a 17:50.7 at the WACC Championship at Hayward High, 18:17.8 at the CIF State Championship in Fresno, and 18:44.4 at the Capital Cross Challenge in Sacramento. In spite of the winter weather in Pennsylvania, she is happy to be running again. “I am definitely enjoying Pittsburgh and the East Coast. Fall is incredible because the leaves turn colors and the entire park is a vibrant red and yellow, which we don’t see as much in California. I’m still adjusting to the cold, but I really like experiencing seasons,” said Zalewski. Already eying 2022, she’s eager to continue her progress from the lengthy foot injury and help lead Carnegie Mellon to more success. “I’m regaining fitness and want to come back stronger for next year,” said Zalewski. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse is presenting the musical Into the Woods on stage now through December 23. The show premiered on November 19 after a year and a half hiatus due to COVID-19. Into the Woods tells the story of a baker and his wife who attempt to lift a family curse and have a child. They are visited by a witch who promises she can fulfill the request, but on her terms only. The couple must travel into the nearby woods and search for four items: a cow as white as milk, a cape as red as blood, hair as yellow as corn, and a slipper as pure as gold. The production features a cast of familiar fairytale characters, including Rapunzel, Cinderella, Jack, and Little Red Riding Hood. Music and lyrics are by Stephen Sondheim for this play adaption of James Lapine’s book of the same name. The play is directed by Alex Rodriguez, with Anthony Rollins-Mullens as narrator. The show stars Alexis Lazear, Reggie White, and Rebecca Pingree in the lead roles. To purchase tickets, visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse. org.

articles.text: B.B. King had a great blues education. The Reverend Archie Fair showed B.B. his first chords (I, IV and V) on a $15 Silvertone guitar Rev. Fair bought from Sears Roebuck. B.B. was seven. His favorite musicians in his youth were Blind Lemon Jefferson and Lonnie Johnson. B.B.’s mother’s first cousin, Bukka White, recorded on Victor and Vocalion records. B.B. loved Bukka’s bottleneck slide guitar tone and later fashioned the shimmering sound into his famous vibrato. He bought his first guitar, a Stella acoustic, at age twelve and taught himself to play scales and read music a little with a Nick Manaloft book from Sears. B.B. played on Son Boy Williamson II’s KWEM in West Memphis, then on KDIA, Memphis. At KDIA he was a singer and DJ, first called “Beale Street Blues Boy”, later shortened to “B.B.”. After hearing T-Bone there, B.B. had to get an electric guitar. As a DJ in the forties, B.B. heard lots of musicians (after the army in ’44-’45). His influences include T-Bone Walker, Oscar Moore, Charlie Christian, Django Reinhardt, and Tiny Grimes. B.B. felt he couldn’t play chords well and performed solely as a singer and single-note guitar improviser. Ike Turner introduced B.B. to the recording industry. In 1952, his “3 O’Clock Blues” was number one on the Billboard R&B charts. After many 1950’s hits including “Every Day I Have the Blues” and “Sweet Little Angel”, B.B. became popular among sixties rock artists including Clapton and the Stones. Although B.B. studied scales as a kid, he built his style on licks and phrases he picked up from guitarists and vocalists. He thought vocally in conceiving phrases. Analyzing B.B.’s solos academically shows bits of different scales. He’d use a few notes of minor pentatonic (C-Eb-F-G-Bb in C) and of major pentatonic (C-D-E-G-A in C) in the same phrase. A phrase might use C minor pentatonic, yet end on the “A” from C major pentatonic. B.B. phrased with breaths like a vocalist. His signature style includes his shimmering vibrato (often while a note is picked repeatedly), a single high-pitched “button” note for emphasis and a wide-range bent note played on an offbeat. Use the link below to see and hear my improvisations in B.B.’s Style: www.guitarimprov. com/B.B.King’sFortiesRoots.pdf His guitar was named after a woman fought in a brawl at a dance where B.B. performed and the two men knocked over a lit barrel of kerosene. In the ensuing fire, B.B. retrieved his guitar and named it “Lucille”. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Stuart Canin remains – master of all he surveys. That’s the stuff dreams are made of. At the tender age of 95, Stuart Canin was in full commend of his instrument. articles.text: Finding Nemo is a computer-generated Pixar film that debuted in 2003 and was an instant hit. This animated film greeted a whole new generation of youngsters, eager to engage in an adventurous search for a small clownfish named Nemo (Alex Gould) who has gone missing. This orange, white, black striped little guy lives in the Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Australia. His father is Marlin (Albert Brooks), his mother Coral (Elizabeth Perkins). She has recently laid a number of eggs, but as it turns out all but one are damaged during a barracuda attack. The lone survivor is Nemo. Marlin is, of course, overprotective of his only little clownfish son. But Nemo rebels. He decides to swim but is too close to a speedboat and is captured by scuba divers. Marlin, aghast, tries to follow the boat, but in vain. He meets up with Dory (Ellen DeGeneres), a blue tang fish, who apparently suffers from shortterm memory loss, but still offers to help Marlin find Nemo. And thus begins the quest – at times frantic – to find Nemo, who has been taken to live in an aquarium in a Sydney dentist’s office (Bill Hunter). Nemo quickly realizes that he is not alone, but has the company of what is referred to as “the tank gang”: there’s Bubbles, a yellow tang fish (Stephen Root); Peaches, a starfish (Allison Janey); shrimp Jacques (Joe Ranft); idol fish Gil (Willem Dafoe); Bloat the Blowfish (Brad Garnett); royal gramma Gurgle; and damselfish Deb (Vicki Lewis). articles.text: I met Randy and Krys Wulff 20 years ago when I first moved to Piedmont. We would see each other at church but it was only when they went into the wine business that I really got to know them. After successful careers in law and arbitration (Randy) and optometry consultation (Krys) they decided to start a winery. They bought a house and vineyard in Napa Valley and at first mostly sold their grapes to other high-quality producers. Then they relocated to a house on Atlas Peak with a killer view of the valley. They began planting Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Petite Verdot in 1995 on an estate vineyard surrounding the house, and Lobo Atlas Peak was off and running. As the vines aged the wines improved each year. The Wulffs hired talented UC Davis educated, Frenchtrained winemaker Victoria Coleman and veteran vineyard manager Mario Bazan to round out the team. Everything seemed to be going great until October 8, 2017 – the Atlas Peak Fire. Krys was out of town and when Randy woke in the middle of the night he saw a wall of flames bearing down on the house. He managed to escape with the two cats and nothing else. The house and guest house burned to the ground but most of the vineyard managed to survive. It has been four years now and like a phoenix, a new improved house and guest house have risen from the ashes. The property has such a beauty and serenity now it is hard to imagine the destruction that was wreaked upon this place. Grapes are amazing plants. There is an old saying…if you have a piece of land so poor that absolutely nothing will grow – plant grapes. They are tough guys. So maybe it is not surprising that a fire that decimated everything but the chimney could not destroy the vineyards. The grapes from the Lobo Atlas Estate vineyard are producing at the top of their form. In addition to the new vineyard. the Wulffs continue to produce wine from their original valley floor vineyard. In fact, this year Lobo Vineyards went from small, family-owned, little-known winery to small, family-owned, winery on the cover of Decanter magazine. That’s right, this year Decanter listed Lobo Napa Valley as one of California’s top Cabernet Sauvignons. Quite an honor to say the least. Several years ago Lobo joined with a couple of other wineries to develop a state of the art winery and tasting room called The Caves at Soda Canyon. They offer fantastic tasting experiences with amazing views of Napa Valley from the terrace. Appointments can be made by visiting the website www.lobowines.com • or calling 707-224-8322. Wine purchases are best made directly from the winery via the website. 2020 Lobo Chardonnay The 2020 Lobo Chardonnay is a beauty. Ripe, concentrated and fresh, with lots of golden fruits, a touch of oak, crème bruleee and minerality, it’s medium to full-bodied, complex and layered, with a classy, balanced fruit

articles.text: Part 33 in a biweekly series. As I visit cities, towns, and villages in different parts of the world, the thing I enjoy most is walking through the downtowns, Distinctive landmarks traditionally punctuate the core of a city, such as these church towers in Ljubljana, the relatively small capital city of Slovenia. Besides their aesthetic appeal, they keep us in touch with the local history, while at the same time providing orientation and wayfinding for both pedestrians and autos. Public spaces of town centers don’t have to be (in fact should not be) very big to form a truly energized, vital core area where people come together and interact. This proposed small city plaza in Mexico is designed purposely tight to the surrounding shops, restaurants, and commercial uses to facilitate a synergistic and exciting environment. the cores, the centers. In fact, I would say the value of these areas is the most important thing I have learned after decades of observation and practice in the various fields of environmental design. They define the heart of a place. Always easily recognizable by the change of use from private to public, the change of building size and type, and the resulting increased pedestrian activity, there is a whole different feeling and energy associated with even the smallest scale successful center. It brings with it a sense that you have arrived, that this is the gathering place, the heart of the community. In a larger context like the Bay Area, the city of San Francisco itself could describe the core. In huge Mexico City, the Centro Histórico (Zocalo) neighborhood is considered by most to be the heart and soul of the metropolis. And in a small California town like Healdsburg, the beautiful little town square is clearly, as Gertrude Stein might have described it, the “there” there. In the end, what makes town centers successful is how well they provide for and enhance the various aspects of public life. They include a mix of civic, commercial, recreational, and residential uses that are designed in such a way to facilitate interaction among people. In short, they foster community. This incredibly important concept is universal, with continuous historic precedent: from the bustling, agoras in ancient Greece, to the civic plazas in Europe and South America to, (what were) the exciting “downtowns” across the USA…to…unfortunately, the weak imitators like shopping malls surrounded by huge parking lots of our era. In Piedmont, the town center is obvious as the residential pattern changes to the collection of public buildings and public spaces located in the geographical middle of the town. In my mind, “public” buildings include not only the civic buildings, like the city hall and schools, but also commercial, and religious buildings which although not publicly owned, take on the same role as venues for bringing people together. Included in this mix is Piedmont Center for the Arts with its exhibits and performances as an energizer and community enhancer, and soon the new theater being built at the high school will do the same. One great advantage of the small size of our relatively dense core is the ease of walking between uses and functions – the exact opposite of the familiar contemporary pattern of single uses surrounded by huge parking lots. How successful is Piedmont’s town center? What do you think? Many successful components are in place here, working pretty well

articles.text: Winnie Wong and her guzheng. Winnie Wong delighted Lake Park Senior Community residents with a live concert on October 27. Wong began her training on the guzheng in 1982 at the age of four and a half under the expertise of guzheng virtuoso, Ms. Weishan Liu. At age 5, she had her debut and immediately developed a deep bond with the guzheng and its culture. Dear Macmama: My wife and I just updated our will and trust, but I feel like I should make other preparations. For example, should I give my passwords to my kids, so they can access my computer when I pass away? –Allen P., Oakland Dear Allen: The more that you can prepare your family members for the event of your passing, the easier time they will have with the immense work involved in settling an estate. I know that most of us work hard to make sure we have all our financial affairs in order so our beneficiaries will have an easier time when we pass, but there are so many things in our digital life that we don’t think of. One of my nephews, who works in cyber security says that each person should create a digital “If I Go Missing” folder that contains all our important passwords and phone numbers. Things like our email passwords, credit card and bank passwords, airlines, shopping and Apple ID to name a few. If you just examine your daily routine, you will be amazed at how many times you must sign in or authenticate to access an account, a website, a subscription or your bank. It’s a good idea to take notes for a week or so, to determine what to add to this folder or document. Now comes the tricky part. If you have a document or a spreadsheet with all this vital information, where can you keep it securely and away from hackers or thieves? Here are a few possibilities: 1. On a piece of paper in a safe. As long as you give the combination to your home safe and let your family members know that this document is there, it’s as safe as anything in your home. Which is to say, it can be stolen or broken into, but still better than in a drawer in your desk. 2. A document on your computer. This is the most common solution and can be encrypted with a password. Again, you must let your family members know how to get into your computer and where this document is stored. But this is not the best solution, as it’s not very secure and often difficult to access when you are not present. 3. In a Google Doc. I know that many folks keep private info in a Google document, limiting access by only sharing access with family members. Google’s servers are as secure as most cloud suites, but not meant for ultra-secure data. This also has setbacks, not so much because there is a security issue, but there is too much room for user error. 4. On password management software like 1Password, or LastPass. These are my choice, since they offer the opportunity to create “family vaults”. In the case of 1Password, you can add another “family organizer” so they have access to your account in case you can’t sign in or pass away. LastPass also has levels of access that you can allow other users. What about accessing your iPhone and iPad? Apple has finally provided a new feature in the soon to be released iOS 15.2 for your iPhone and iPad, that promises help for family members trying to wrestle with your data after you are gone. As of this new update (to be released sometime soon), you will be able to add Legacy Contacts, trusted people who can access your Apple ID and your devices in the event of your death. After providing a death certificate, these contacts will be provided an access key to download all your data. Of course, this will include everything, so make sure you really trust them! As our lives become more technically involved, so must our preparation for access to this technology postmortem. And as one who has struggled to settle the estate of a loved one, and been frustrated with no access to necessary passwords for the countless accounts we had to close, I have become committed to making sure my own family will have an easier time after I am gone. articles.text: Being a caregiver for a loved one can be rewarding and fulfilling, even renewing relationships later in life. However, depending on the illness that someone is living with, caregiving can also be physically and emotionally draining and lead to health issues for a well-meaning caregiver. A look at the numbers In a recent report from Blue Cross-Blue Shield, 57% of caregivers were found to be “experiencing clinically significant levels of stress, anxiety or depression.”. During the peak of the COVID- 19 pandemic in 2020, the report found that 1 in 4 caregivers were “feeling more stress trying to balance work and family.” The Family Caregiver Alliance provides a variety of statistics on caregiving pulled from many sources. They note several interesting facts, including: • That caregiving spouses have poorer health than other types of family caregivers • That older caregivers—those over age 65—rate a physical strain of caregiving as “high” • That caregivers for someone who is living with Alzheimer’s • disease or dementia also rate a physical strain of caregiving as “high” 40% to 70% of family caregivers have clinically significant symptoms of depression. But why? Family members often jump into caregiving with no experience or training. Caregiving for a loved one can start out small, doing a few favors or helping out here and there. Then, as a progressive illness such as dementia worsens and the needs for their assistance increase, the stress can also increase. In some instances, a loved one has time to be a companion to an elder who just needs a little company and help driving to the grocery store. However, some conditions require physical help such as lifting someone in and out of bed or the tub and this can cause injuries to the caregiver. When someone has a progressive illness that leads to a deterioration in their abilities to take care of their own daily activities, it can lead to a family member taking on more and more personal care for which they are unprepared, as well as the emotional stress of watching their parent or spouse changing. It is important for these caregivers to avoid burnout and injury; the toll of caregiving on health worsens over time. Professional care with a trained caregiver can augment a family caregiver’s efforts and potentially reduce stress and the chance of illness. For some people in need of assistance, it takes a care team. Being aware of the risks of caring for a family member is important so that caregivers can seek out the support they need to maintain their own wellness. Support groups (in-person or virtual), training, and other longterm care options can be considered to decrease stress on a family caregiver. articles.text: Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr. died on November 12 at age 85. Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr., father of John C. Weaver III and son of Violet Jurs Weaver and John Carrel Weaver, passed away at Highland Hospital on November 12, 2021, where he had once served his medical residency. He was 85. Born on August 12, 1936, he lived in the Rockridge neighborhood until moving to Piedmont in 1942. In 1954 he graduated from Piedmont High School, went on to graduate from Stanford University, followed by medical school at Northwestern University. He served his internship at Highland Hospital in Oakland from 1962 to 1963. Following that he served on active duty as a physician with the Marine Corps in Okinawa and Japan. He returned to serve his medical residency at Highland Hospital, followed by a fellowship in Nephrology at San Francisco General Hospital (UCSF) from 1968 to 1969. He joined what became the Oakland Medical Group in 1969, and in 1970 started the Chronic Hemodialysis Program at Providence Hospital in Oakland. He was the first physician to provide dialysis services in the East Bay. de la Raza in Oakland, the West Oakland Community Health Center and rural clinics in Tuolumne, Copperopolis and Garberville, California. A lifelong learner, he studied Spanish to better serve his patients. He enjoyed exploring the world. His travels took him to six of the seven continents, highlighted by his time in Japan, where he studied the language and toured the country extensively by train, visiting Hiroshima and Nagasaki and climbing Mount Fujiyama. He also visited Hong Kong, Thailand and the Philippines. As a boy, he participated in athletics. After winning the Piedmont Junior High School free-throw shooting championship at age 13, he participated in high school football and basketball, predominantly warming the bench and “hoping the coach might send me in, but more afraid he might.” His community involvements and club memberships included the Piedmont Community Church, Alameda-Contra Costa Medical Association, the Claremont Country Club and 50 years as a member of Oakland Rotary Club. Through Rotary, he visited all the Central American countries for international projects with the World Community Service Committee. In addition to travel, John enjoyed fishing, duck hunting and golf. A lifelong embracer of conservative ideals, he proudly flew the American flag from his porch railing above the Oakland Estuary. John is predeceased by his parents and by his former wife, Brenda Best Weaver. He is survived by his son, John C. Weaver III, of San Francisco, sisters Stephanie Mooers of Piedmont and Julie Weaver Jurs of Portland, Oregon. He also leaves behind nieces and nephews Michael Mooers of Grass Valley, Jeff Mooers of Lafayette, and Tom Mooers of Sierra City. He is also survived by nephews and nieces Justin Anderson, Mary Kate Horwood, Emily Anderson Johnson and Jennifer Garcia Navarro, all of the Seattle, Washington area. He later worked with East Bay Nephrology Group and Santa Rosa Medical Clinic in Coachella, CA. A generous volunteer, he traveled extensively to bring his medical skills to underserved areas in California and around the world. articles.text: Barbara Fox Roach passed away peacefully in her sleep in her beloved Piedmont home on Monday, November 8, 2021, after a courageous six-month battle with cancer. She lived a long, extraordinary life, capped by the celebration of her 90th birthday in June. Barbara was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on June 2, 1931, the youngest of seven siblings and the only daughter of John Raymond Fox and Elsie Warren Fox. Despite an age difference that spanned 21 years, she remained close to all of her brothers: Les, Joe, Art, Gil, Gene, and Jerry. Her childhood years were a challenge during the Depression, but growing up on a ranch helped shape Barbara into the ambitious, determined, and courageous young woman she became. At the age of thirteen, she moved in with another family, where she earned her room and board as a nanny and house cleaner until her graduation from Sheridan High School in 1949. Barbara attended Cottey College in Missouri, then transferred to the University of Wyoming, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in English in 1953 and was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. Barbara then moved west to San Francisco and became a stewardess for United Airlines. At a time when commercial flying was still in its nascency, she enjoyed long, friendly encounters with the likes of Walt Disney, Gregory Peck, and John Steinbeck. It was in San Francisco where she met the first love of her life, Justin M. Roach Jr., while Justin was attending Stanford Law School. They married in San Francisco in 1959 and then moved to Piedmont in 1960, where they raised their family and lived the rest of their lives. Justin began a long and distinguished legal career with the Oakland law firm that would eventually become Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. Barbara and Justin enjoyed a 28-year marriage until Justin’s death in 1987. In 2005, Barbara met the second love of her life, Arne share her observations through colorful vignettes of people and events. She also possessed a steady and insatiable curiosity in past and present issues – a trait cultivated by years of traveling the world with experts and loved ones. Not surprisingly, she had numerous interests and hobbies that ranged from orchid growing and needlepointing to playing tennis and golf. She remained an avid reader of fiction and nonfiction throughout her life and loved the opera as much as she loved a crisp, morning walk. Few could ever keep pace with her, even in her later years. Barbara was devoted to her four children, Justin Roach III (Dianne Peebles Roach), Kristin Roach Roeth (George), Steven Roach (Erica Heinsen) and David Roach (Christi Nielsen). “Barbar” loved and adored her eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren: Jessica Roach, Justin Roach IV, and James Roach; Justin (Hank) Roeth, Megan Roeth, Jack Roeth and Everett Roeth; Emmett Roach and Renée Roach; Dillon Roach and Nathan Nielsen, and the newest additions to the family tree, Jeanette Roeth and Justin Henry Roeth II. She was the matriarch of a large, loving family that will always remember her for her courage, fortitude, love, and grace. Barbara’s family is eternally grateful for the love and support of all of Barbara’s close friends who were by her side physically and spiritually these last several months. In particular, the family would like to extend its profound thanks and deep appreciation to Amy McClaskey and Elizabeth Vigo, who were her companions and caregivers until the very end. A private memorial service and celebration of life for family and friends is planned for January 8, 2022. Dr. John Carrel Weaver, Jr., father of John C. Weaver III and son of Violet Jurs Weaver and John Carrel Weaver, passed away at Highland Hospital on November 12, 2021, where he had once served his medical residency. He was 85. Born on August 12, 1936, he lived in the Rockridge neighborhood until moving to Piedmont in 1942. In 1954 he graduated from Piedmont High School, went on to graduate from Stanford University, followed by medical school at Northwestern University. He served his internship at Highland Hospital in Oakland from 1962 to 1963. Following that he served on active duty as a physician with the Marine Corps in Okinawa and Japan. He returned to serve his medical residency at Highland Hospital, followed by a fellowship in Nephrology at San Francisco General Hospital (UCSF) from 1968 to 1969. He joined what became the Oakland Medical Group in 1969, and in 1970 started the Chronic Hemodialysis Program at Providence Hospital in Oakland. He was the first physician to provide dialysis services in the East Bay. de la Raza in Oakland, the West Oakland Community Health Center and rural clinics in Tuolumne, Copperopolis and Garberville, California. A lifelong learner, he studied Spanish to better serve his patients. He enjoyed exploring the world. His travels took him to six of the seven continents, highlighted by his time in Japan, where he studied the language and toured the country extensively by train, visiting Hiroshima and Nagasaki and climbing Mount Fujiyama. He also visited Hong Kong, Thailand and the Philippines. As a boy, he participated in athletics. After winning the Piedmont Junior High School free-throw shooting championship at age 13, he participated in high school football and basketball, predominantly warming the bench and “hoping the coach might send me in, but more afraid he might.” His community involvements and club memberships included the Piedmont Community Church, Alameda-Contra Costa Medical Association, the Claremont Country Club and 50 years as a member of Oakland Rotary Club. Through Rotary, he visited all the Central American countries for international projects with the World Community Service Committee. In addition to travel, John enjoyed fishing, duck hunting and golf. A lifelong embracer of conservative ideals, he proudly flew the American flag from his porch railing above the Oakland Estuary. John is predeceased by his parents and by his former wife, Brenda Best Weaver. He is survived by his son, John C. Weaver III, of San Francisco, sisters Stephanie Mooers of Piedmont and Julie Weaver Jurs of Portland, Oregon. He also leaves behind nieces and nephews Michael Mooers of Grass Valley, Jeff Mooers of Lafayette, and Tom Mooers of Sierra City. He is also survived by nephews and nieces Justin Anderson, Mary Kate Horwood, Emily Anderson Johnson and Jennifer Garcia Navarro, all of the Seattle, Washington area. He later worked with East Bay Nephrology Group and Santa Rosa Medical Clinic in Coachella, CA. A generous volunteer, he traveled extensively to bring his medical skills to underserved areas in California and around the world. His work took him to Thailand, American Samoa, Cambodia, Malawi and Peru. She lived a long, extraordinary life, capped by the celebration of her 90th birthday in June. Barbara was born in Sheridan, Wyoming on June 2, 1931, the youngest of seven siblings and the only daughter of John Raymond Fox and Elsie Warren Fox. Despite an age difference that spanned 21 years, she remained close to all of her brothers: Les, Joe, Art, Gil, Gene, and Jerry. Her childhood years were a challenge during the Depression, but growing up on a ranch helped shape Barbara into the ambitious, determined, and courageous young woman she became. At the age of thirteen, she moved in with another family, where she earned her room and board as a nanny and house cleaner until her graduation from Sheridan High School in 1949. Barbara attended Cottey College in Missouri, then transferred to the University of Wyoming, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in English in 1953 and was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. Barbara then moved west to San Francisco and became a stewardess for United Airlines. At a time when commercial flying was still in its nascency, she enjoyed long, friendly encounters with the likes of Walt Disney, Gregory Peck, and John Steinbeck. It was in San Francisco where she met the first love of her life, Justin M. Roach Jr., while Justin was attending Stanford Law School. They married in San Francisco in 1959 and then moved to Piedmont in 1960, where they raised their family and lived the rest of their lives. Justin began a long and distinguished legal career with the Oakland law firm that would eventually become Crosby, Heafey, Roach & May. Barbara and Justin enjoyed a 28-year marriage until Justin’s death in 1987. In 2005, Barbara met the second love of her life, Arne share her observations through colorful vignettes of people and events. She also possessed a steady and insatiable curiosity in past and present issues – a trait cultivated by years of traveling the world with experts and loved ones. Not surprisingly, she had numerous interests and hobbies that ranged from orchid growing and needlepointing to playing tennis and golf. She remained an avid reader of fiction and nonfiction throughout her life and loved the opera as much as she loved a crisp, morning walk. Few could ever keep pace with her, even in her later years. Barbara was devoted to her four children, Justin Roach III (Dianne Peebles Roach), Kristin Roach Roeth (George), Steven Roach (Erica Heinsen) and David Roach (Christi Nielsen). “Barbar” loved and adored her eleven grandchildren and two great grandchildren: Jessica Roach, Justin Roach IV, and James Roach; Justin (Hank) Roeth, Megan Roeth, Jack Roeth and Everett Roeth; Emmett Roach and Renée Roach; Dillon Roach and Nathan Nielsen, and the newest additions to the family tree, Jeanette Roeth and Justin Henry Roeth II. She was the matriarch of a large, loving family that will always remember her for her courage, fortitude, love, and grace. Barbara’s family is eternally grateful for the love and support of all of Barbara’s close friends who were by her side physically and spiritually these last several months. In particular, the family would like to extend its profound thanks and deep appreciation to Amy McClaskey and Elizabeth Vigo, who were her companions and caregivers until the very end. A private memorial service and celebration of life for family and friends is planned for January 8, 2022. Donations in Barbara’s memory may be made to the Oakland Zoo, the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West, or a charity of choice. The two enjoyed 10 wonderful years together, traveling the world, vacationing at their homes in Carmel and Palm Desert, and playing golf with friends at Claremont Country Club in Oakland and Monterey Peninsula Country Club in Pebble Beach, until Arne’s passing in 2016. A life-long Republican and philanthropist, Barbara contributed to numerous charitable, community, and political organizations, including the Cancer League, the Oakland Museum, the Russian National Orchestra, the San Francisco Opera, the Oakland Symphony, the Oakland Zoo, and the Buffalo Bill Center of the Wild West in Cody, Wyoming. As a member of the board of the Oakland Zoo, Barbara played an important role in the zoo’s fundraising efforts and its transformation into a world-class institution. Her passion for politics eventually led her to work on the re-election campaign of Pete Wilson to the U.S. Senate and to become a member of the Lincoln Club of Northern California and the Media Research Group. articles.text: Helen Cecile Peoples Buty peacefully passed away on October 30. Born in Hankow, China in 1929, she was the daughter of Lewis Jackson Peoples and Marguerite Ann Tahaney. Helen was a wife, mother, friend, business woman, athlete and world traveler. She spent her early childhood in China, but with the onset of World War II, the family was forced to return to San Francisco. When her father was released from Santo Tomas Internment Camp, the family settled in Louisburg, North Carolina, and then Washington DC. Helen attended Western High School and American University, where she was a member of Delta Gamma sorority, the debate team as well as a varsity swimmer where she won a collegiate medal. Helen was the youngest woman to join the Red Cross and during the Korean Conflict was stationed in Pusan, South Korea. Upon her return, she became a secretary at Kaiser Permanente and helped to develop their centralized patient admissions system. She was married to Francis Helen enjoyed world travel. She cruised the seven seas and visited every continent with her family and friends. Helen excelled at sports, and especially loved tennis which she played until the spry age of 82. When Helen wasn’t traveling, working, playing tennis, dominoes or bridge she was entertaining. She was a gracious hostess and fabulous cook. Her home was open to those in need of a place to stay, strangers and friends alike. Many family friends enjoyed extended stays at the Buty family home. Helen is survived by son Louis, his wife K, daughters Mary and Madeline, and their husbands Rick and Jason. She is also survived by grandchildren, Gina, Joe, Wynton and Zachary and by six nephews, two nieces, several cousins as well as grandnieces and grandnephews. articles.text: William Henry Fraley, born February 15, 1928, to Ferdinand and Marion Saphir Fraley, died peacefully on November 4, 2021, after 93 eventful and unforgettable years. Known as Bill to all who loved and knew him, he grew up in Piedmont, graduating from Piedmont High School in 1946 and later from the University of California at Berkeley. He married the lovely Patsy Craig in 1953, served as a Lieutenant in the U.S. Army in France in the mid 1950’s, and then settled into a long and successful career as a Planning Commissioner for Alameda County. Bill and Patsy lived their entire lives together in Piedmont. Bill was a wonderfully unique character – funny, and with a bemused and unpredictable view of the world around him and everyone in it. Bill was “old school,” a can-do, get-it-done kind of guy with a personality that filled the room wherever he went. Bill was a consummate outdoorsman and Gold Country historian. He was a back-country fisherman, high Sierra backpacker and cross-country trekker, and the creator and driver of the Yubierra cabin retreat in the Gold Country at Goodyear Bar, providing more than 50 years of enormous pleasure to his family and friends. Such good times there. Bill was an avid cyclist and will always be remembered for his screaming downhill runs at the Markleeville Death Ride and many similar places. Whatever the difficulty or downturn of any life adventure, Bill bore it with a grin and a solution. articles.text: On Thursday, December 2, the City of Piedmont will host a virtual Housing Element Community Workshop at 5:30 p.m. In the creation of the 2023- 2031 Housing Element, which is a chapter of the General Plan, the City of Piedmont will consider all types of land uses, housing types, building types and heights, residential densities, code changes, and housing programs, such as subsidies and incentives, in order to meet the state-mandated goal of accommodating 587 new housing units by 2031 and to affirmatively further fair housing in Piedmont. Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson noted, “All options for new housing units must be on the table because accessory dwelling units alone will not be enough to meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation.” Community members interested in participating can access the workshop in the following ways: • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont-cagov.zoom.us/j/85005754222 • Computer or smart phone: Click on https://piedmont. • • ca.gov/government/meeting_ videos Telephone: Dial (669) 900- 9128 and enter webinar/meeting number 850-0575-4222 Television: Watch on KCOM, Comcast Channel 27 or AT&T UVerse Channel 99 Register before the meeting to be entered for a raffle prize drawing at https://bit.ly/community_wskp_1 In addition to the device being used to participate in the meeting, participants are asked to have a smartphone in hand for live polling during the virtual workshop.

According to Mamuyac, another advantage of Concept C is that the design lends itself to an entry plaza level. At the end of the evening, attendees gave ELS a “resounding direction to move forward on Concept C,” he said. This was the second workshop in a series of three being hosted by the architect firm. The final workshop will be held on Tuesday, December 14, at 7 p.m. ELS will present a final draft program and a refined Concept C. Guests will be given the opportunity to join small tabletop design teams that will critique and evaluate the concept. Following that workshop, ELS and city staff will collect and record findings from each team and synthesize data into a final concept. The preferred direction will be presented to the city council in early 2022. Council Member Betsy Andersen, who attended both community workshops, noted the large turnout on November 16, with more than 80 people in attendance. “I am delighted that ELS Architecture and Urban Design was able to use the conceptual design from 2016 as a launch pad for these community workshops. Since we only have one pool facility for our residents, time is of the essence to get it rebuilt,” said Andersen, who was integral in the 2020 Yes on Measure UU campaign. The measure passed with a two-thirds majority of yes vote in November 2020, allowing the city to issue up to $19.5 million in bonds with bond revenue going to fund a new aquatic complex. Anderson noted that both workshops were attended by Olympic swimmers Dana Vollmer Grant, who works for ELS, and her friend and former Olympic and Cal teammate, Nathan Adrian, who lives in the East Bay and teaches swim lessons. “Judging from the great turnout at these workshops, the community is eager to help move this project forward. Talking about options for the new design truly is the fun part. We are in great hands with ELS, as they have tons of experience building stateof-the-art community pools in California,” Andersen said.
